bottomLine: The law speaks until every mouth is closed and the whole world stands guilty before God. No one is righteous, not even the best performers of the law. That silence is not the end. It is where a man stops arguing and starts asking for grace.
benediction: Brother, the dust keeps a man talking — explaining, defending, comparing, producing his record like exhibits before a judge — because as long as the mouth is open, he can keep believing he might still win his case. Lift your eyes off your own defense. The Law has been speaking, and one by one it has taken away your arguments, until there is nothing left to say but the truth: guilty, with no defense of your own. Do not be afraid of that silence. The silenced mouth is not the loser’s mouth. It is the praying mouth, the one finally free to stop arguing for merit and start asking for grace.

So when the Law silences you this week and the old reflex wants to reopen the case, lift up your eyes. When you catch yourself ranking against other men, lift up your eyes — even the best of them fell short, and the contest is over. When the verdict lands and feels like the end of all hope, lift up your eyes, because the very next word after the gavel is grace. The same Paul who wrote “every mouth stopped” wrote, two verses later, “But now apart from the law, a righteousness of God has been revealed.” The accountability was never the destination. It was the threshold. Jesus stood in the dock you deserve, took the verdict that was yours, and bore the curse of the Law you could never keep, so that in the silence after your defense runs out, God could speak over you the only word that matters.

This is from dust to revival — not a man arguing his way to acquittal, but a man whose case has finally run out, who stops talking and at last can hear. The tax collector beat his breast, said only “be merciful to me, a sinner,” and went home justified, while the man still listing his merits went home with his case unheard. Lift up your eyes off your own defense and onto the One who became your defense. Let the mouth close. Let the verdict land. And then listen — because in the holy quiet, grace is about to speak. Welcome to week four, where the silence becomes a doorway.
closingVerse: Your soul clings to the dust with nothing left to say in its own defense. Lift up your eyes — the silence after the gavel is where grace finally speaks.
carry: What defense do you need to stop making?

pulls: After the longest indictment in Scripture come the two words that change everything: but now. The burden does not get lighter — it gets lifted onto Another.
paras: Where the Dust Lifts at Last For four weeks the road has run downhill. You have watched the rich young ruler walk away sorrowful, felt the Stone under your own feet, looked into the mirror that could only show the dust and never wash it, and heard the Law speak until every mouth fell silent and the whole world stood guilty in the dock. If the study had stopped there, it would have been honest, but it would have been unbearable. A man cannot live under a verdict with no appeal. But the study does not stop there — because Romans does not stop there. After the longest, hardest indictment in all of Scripture come two words that turn the whole world around.

But now. “But now apart from the law, a righteousness of God has been revealed” (Romans 3:21). For three chapters Paul has been building the case against you — and then, with the gavel still ringing in the air, he pivots on two small words and announces that everything has changed. The righteousness you could never produce by the Law has appeared from another source entirely, apart from the Law, as a gift. The mouth that was stopped by the verdict is opened again — not to argue, but to receive. This is the hinge of the whole Bible, and the hinge of this whole study. Everything before it was setup. Everything after it is grace.

If you have felt the weight of the last four weeks, this is the week it lifts. Not because you finally performed well enough — you did not, and you could not — but because God did, in Christ, what you never could. The burden does not lift by being made lighter. It lifts by being taken off your back entirely and laid on Another. This is the week you stop talking about what you cannot do and start declaring what He has done. But now. Lift your eyes; the long descent is over, and the ground beneath you just became grace.

The Two Words the Ruler Needed to Hear Remember the disciples’ astonished question when the rich young ruler walked away: “Then who can be saved?” If a man that good could not make it, what hope is there for anyone? And Jesus answered with the sentence this whole study is built on: “With men it is impossible, but not with God, for all things are possible with God” (Mark 10:27). Hear how perfectly that lands here. With man it is impossible — that is Romans 1 through 3, the silenced mouth, the whole world guilty, salvation by works exposed as hopeless. But with God — that is Romans 3:21, the but now, the righteousness of God breaking in from outside, doing the impossible thing.

This is why the impossibility was never bad news. The moment a man stops resisting the impossibility — stops insisting that with enough effort he could pull it off — is the exact moment he is positioned to hear “but with God.” As long as he thinks salvation is merely difficult, he keeps running. When he finally accepts that it is impossible, he looks up, and there is the gift, held out to him by the God for whom all things are possible. The ruler’s tragedy is that he turned away one sentence too soon. He heard “With men it is impossible” and left grieving, and never stayed to hear “but with God.” Do not make his mistake. Stay for the second half of the sentence. It is where the whole gospel lives.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: Apart From the Law
paras: Mark the phrase: the righteousness of God has been revealed “apart from the law” (Romans 3:21). Not by improving the Law, not by lowering its standard, not by grading the Law on a curve — apart from it altogether. This is a righteousness from a completely different source than human performance. It does not come up from the ground of your effort; it comes down from heaven as a gift. Every other religion and every instinct of the human heart says righteousness must be built from below, brick by brick, deed by deed. The gospel says it has already been finished above and handed down, complete, to be received.

This is the death of the works-road and the birth of rest in the same breath. If righteousness comes apart from the Law, then your failures on the Law cannot disqualify you and your successes on the Law cannot purchase you — because the whole transaction is happening on different ground. The man who grasps “apart from the law” stops frantically auditing his performance, because his standing was never going to be settled there. It is settled in Christ, apart from anything he could do or fail to do. The pressure is off, not because the standard dropped, but because Another met it.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: Justified by His Grace as a Gift
paras: Now comes the sentence to write on your heart: you are “being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus” (Romans 3:24). Three words carry the weight. Justified — declared righteous by the Judge, the verdict reversed from guilty to acquitted. Grace — unearned favor, the opposite of wages. Gift — and as if grace were not enough, Paul adds gift, to slam shut every door by which merit might sneak back in. A gift you work for is a wage. A gift you deserve is a payment. This is a gift, freely given, to the guilty.

Feel the contrast with everything that came before. The Sinai vow said we will do, and broke. The ruler asked what shall I do, and walked away. The Law demanded all, and you kept none of it perfectly. And now, into the silence of the stopped mouth, God speaks the opposite of we will do — He has done. The redemption is in Christ Jesus, accomplished, finished, complete, and offered not as a reward to the deserving but as a gift to the bankrupt. You do not earn a gift. You do not deserve a gift. You simply, with empty and open hands, receive it. That is faith — the open hand of a man who has stopped trying to pay.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: How God Stays Just and Justifies the Guilty
paras: There is a problem hidden in the good news, and Paul does not dodge it. How can a just God declare guilty men righteous without becoming unjust Himself? A judge who lets the guilty go free is a corrupt judge. Paul’s answer is the beating heart of the gospel: God put Christ forward “to be an atoning sacrifice, through faith in his blood” so that God might be “just, and the justifier of him who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:25–26). The guilt was not waved away; it was paid. The wrath the verdict required did not evaporate; it fell on Christ. God did not lower the bar — He met it Himself, in His Son, so that the demand of justice and the gift of grace were satisfied in the same act.

This is what makes the gift unshakable. A pardon that ignored justice could be challenged; a pardon purchased in full cannot. The blood of Christ is the receipt stamped paid over your entire debt, and there is no court that can reopen a settled account. So when the dust whispers that grace this free cannot be real, that surely something this costly to God cannot be given to you for nothing, answer it with the cross: it was not nothing. It cost everything — it cost the blood of the Son — and precisely because it cost Him everything, it is given to you for free. The most expensive gift in the universe is the one held out to empty hands.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: From Dust to the Gift
paras: Psalm 119:25 has been your cry from the floor for five weeks: “My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word.” (NKJV) And here, at the hinge of the study, is the word that revives. It is not do more. It is but now. Revival, for a man crushed under a verdict he cannot appeal, comes not when he finally performs his way off the floor, but when grace reaches down to the floor and lifts him by a righteousness that was never his own. The dust is exactly where the gift is given — not to men who climbed out of it, but to men still lying in it with empty, open hands.

So this week, if you have carried the weight of the last four, set it down. The verdict was real, but the verdict was not the end. But now the righteousness of God has appeared, apart from the Law, as a gift, through the blood of Christ, to all who believe. You are not asked to produce it; you are asked to receive it. Stop trying to pay for what has already been bought. Open your hands. Lift your eyes off your own bankruptcy and onto the gift held out to you, and hear God say over the guilty, silenced, dust-clinging man what He could never have said in answer to your performance: justified — freely, by grace, as a gift, in Christ. Welcome to the day the burden lifted.

stations.verse: But now apart from the law, a righteousness of God has been revealed, being testified by the law and the prophets; even the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ to all and on all those who believe. For there is no distinction,
stations.question: Where am I still trying to build righteousness from the ground up by my effort, when God has handed it down as a finished gift in Christ?
stations.gloss: now, at this present time
stations.live: When the old verdict presses on you this week, answer it with two words: “But now.”
body: Nyni is a strengthened form of the word for now. “But now apart from the law, a righteousness of God has been revealed.” For three chapters Paul has built the case against every man. Then he turns on two words. There was the time of the verdict, and there is now, the time when God’s righteousness has been shown in Christ. The indictment was real. It was not the last word.

stations.verse: being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus;
stations.question: Do I treat my standing with God as a wage I am still earning, or as a gift I have already been given?
stations.gloss: freely, as a gift, without payment
stations.live: Open your hands. The moment you try to pay for the gift, you turn it into a wage.
body: Dōrean means freely — for nothing. Jesus tells His disciples, “Freely you received, so freely give” (Matthew 10:8). Paul says you are “justified freely by his grace.” He piles the words up so no one can smuggle merit back in. You are justified freely: not cheaply, for it cost Christ His blood, but freely to you, with no payment required of the one who receives.

stations.verse: whom God sent to be an atoning sacrifice, through faith in his blood, for a demonstration of his righteousness through the passing over of prior sins, in God’s forbearance;
stations.question: Do I believe God showed His justice at the cross, or do I secretly fear He only looked the other way?
stations.gloss: a showing, a demonstration, proof
stations.live: When you doubt that God could forgive you and stay just, look at the cross. That is the proof.
body: Endeixis is a showing — proof put on display. God sent Christ “for a demonstration of his righteousness,” and Paul repeats the word in the next verse. The cross is not only where God forgave. It is where He showed that He is righteous while He forgives. He did not wink at sin. He put His justice on display at Calvary, so that no man could ever say God simply looked the other way.

stations.verse: whom God sent to be an atoning sacrifice, through faith in his blood, for a demonstration of his righteousness through the passing over of prior sins, in God’s forbearance; to demonstrate his righteousness at this present time; that he might himself be just, and the justifier of him who has faith in Jesus.
stations.question: Does it steady me to know my pardon was not waved through but paid in full — that God stayed just while justifying me?
stations.gloss: forbearance, a holding back of punishment
stations.live: Thank God tonight for the patience that held back what you deserved, and for the cross where it was dealt with.
body: Anochē is forbearance — God holding back what sin deserves. Paul says God passed over prior sins “in God’s forbearance.” He uses the same word when he warns against despising “the riches of his goodness, forbearance, and patience” (Romans 2:4). God’s patience was never indifference. It was waiting. He held back judgment until the cross, where every sin He had passed over was finally answered in His Son.

stations.verse: who was delivered up for our trespasses, and was raised for our justification.
stations.question: Christ was raised for my justification — do I live as a man whose acquittal is already secured, or as one still awaiting the verdict?
stations.gloss: to hand over, to deliver up
stations.live: Read Romans 8:32 before you worry about anything this week. If He gave His Son, He will not hold back what you need.
body: Paradidōmi means to hand someone over. Christ “was delivered up for our trespasses, and was raised for our justification.” Paul says the Father “didn’t spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Romans 8:32). And Paul says the Son “gave himself up for me” (Galatians 2:20). The Father handed Him over, and He handed Himself over. He was delivered for your sin, and raised to declare you righteous.

stations.verse: For him who knew no sin he made to be sin on our behalf; so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.
stations.question: The great exchange — my sin to Christ, His righteousness to me. Am I carrying myself as a man who has become the righteousness of God in Him?

stations.verse: for by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, that no one would boast.
stations.question: Where am I still leaving room to boast — quietly crediting my faith or my effort — when even the faith is a gift?

stations.verse: not by works of righteousness which we did ourselves, but according to his mercy, he saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewing by the Holy Spirit,
stations.question: Can I say it plainly this week — “not by works of righteousness which we did ourselves”?
pulls: With man it is impossible — that is the verdict. But with God all things are possible — that is the gift. Stay for the second half of the sentence.

practices.title: PREACH “BUT NOW” TO THE VERDICT
practices.body: This week, whenever the Law presses a verdict on you — guilty, not enough, behind — answer it with the gospel pivot: “That indictment was real. But now the righteousness of God has appeared, apart from the law, as a gift.” Two words, said out loud against the dust: but now. The verdict was true, but it was never the last word. Train your mouth to follow every accusation with the pivot.

practices.title: OPEN EMPTY HANDS
practices.body: A gift cannot be received by a fist clutching payment. This week, picture yourself coming to God with open, empty hands — no record, no merit, no “yes, but I did this.” Pray: “Lord, I bring nothing to pay for this. I open my hands. I receive what you finished.” The only hands grace fills are the ones that have stopped trying to pay. Practice the open hand until it becomes your posture before God.

practices.title: STAY FOR THE SECOND HALF OF THE SENTENCE
practices.body: Like the ruler, you will be tempted to hear “With men it is impossible” and walk away in despair. Reverse it. When the impossibility of saving yourself lands this week, do not leave — stay and finish the sentence with Jesus: “With me it is impossible. But with you, all things are possible. I am not walking away; I am staying for the grace.” The ruler left one sentence too soon. Do not.

practices.title: LET THE SPIRIT MAKE THE GIFT REAL
practices.body: A gift announced is not the same as a gift enjoyed. This week, ask the Spirit to press the reality of it into your heart: “Holy Spirit, make this gift real to me — not a doctrine I affirm but a freedom I feel. Let me stop paying for what Christ already bought.” The same Spirit who convicted you of the verdict now assures you of the gift; ask Him to do it.

practices.title: TELL A BROTHER WHAT YOU STOPPED PAYING FOR
practices.body: The works-road is relentless, and a man slides back onto it the moment no one is watching. Before the week ends, tell a trusted brother one thing you have been trying to “pay for” with God — some performance you were leaning on — and declare it done: “Christ paid this. I am receiving it free.” Saying it to a brother makes the gift harder to take back onto your own shoulders.

title: But Now
subtitle: from dust to the gift
keyVerse: But now apart from the law, a righteousness of God has been revealed, being testified by the law and the prophets; even the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ to all and on all those who believe. For there is no distinction, for all have sinned, and fall short of the glory of God; being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus;

passage.text: But now apart from the law, a righteousness of God has been revealed, being testified by the law and the prophets;
even the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ to all and on all those who believe. For there is no distinction,
for all have sinned, and fall short of the glory of God;
being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus;
whom God sent to be an atoning sacrifice, through faith in his blood, for a demonstration of his righteousness through the passing over of prior sins, in God’s forbearance;
to demonstrate his righteousness at this present time; that he might himself be just, and the justifier of him who has faith in Jesus.

stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Let the verse land first, then answer honestly — and where a Greek word is opened up, let it sharpen the verse you just prayed over.
lifeIntro: This week is not about earning the gift by Friday. It is about opening empty hands to receive what Christ already finished.
prayer: Father, the verdict against me was just. But now You have shown Your righteousness in Christ. You justify freely, by Your grace, through the blood of Your Son. I have nothing to pay, and I stop trying to pay. Thank You for the patience that held back what I deserved. Let me live this week as a man who was given, not paid. Christ was delivered up for me and raised for me. Amen.
prayerLines: Father, the verdict against me was just.
But now You have shown Your righteousness in Christ.
You justify freely, by Your grace, through the blood of Your Son.
I have nothing to pay, and I stop trying to pay.
Thank You for the patience that held back what I deserved.
Let me live this week as a man who was given, not paid.
Christ was delivered up for me and raised for me. Amen.
bottomLine: “But now” changes everything. A righteousness of God has been revealed apart from the law, and you are justified freely by His grace through the redemption in Christ. God did not look the other way; He showed His justice at the cross, so that He is just and the justifier of him who has faith in Jesus.
benediction: Brother, for four weeks the road ran downhill, and maybe it has felt like the whole study was built to bury you — the ruler walking away, the Stone underfoot, the mirror that could not wash, the verdict that closed every mouth. Lift your eyes, because the descent is over. After the longest indictment ever written, Paul set down two words like a hinge under the whole world: but now. But now the righteousness of God has appeared, apart from the law, as a gift. The weight you have been carrying does not get lighter this week — it gets lifted clean off your back and laid on the shoulders of Another, who carried it to a cross and left it in a tomb.

So when the verdict of the Law presses you down this week, lift up your eyes and say “but now.” When the impossibility of saving yourself finally lands, lift up your eyes and stay for the second half of the sentence — but with God all things are possible. When the dust whispers that grace this free cannot be real, lift up your eyes to the mercy seat, where the blood was offered and the wrath was satisfied and the account was stamped paid, so that God could be both just and the justi.er of guilty men. The ruler heard “With men it is impossible” and walked away grieving, one sentence too soon. Do not leave. The very next word is grace, and it has your name on it.

This is from dust to revival — not a man finally performing his way off the floor, but grace reaching all the way down to the floor and lifting him by a righteousness that was never his own. He was made sin who knew no sin, so that you might become the righteousness of God in Him. That is the great exchange: your guilt onto Christ, His righteousness onto you, the most expensive gift in the universe held out to your empty hands for nothing. Lift up your eyes off your own bankruptcy and onto the gift, and hear the word God speaks over the guilty, silenced, dust-clinging man who simply believes: justified — freely, by grace, as a gift, in Christ. Welcome to week five, the day the burden lifted.
closingVerse: Your soul clings to the dust under a verdict you could never lift. Lift up your eyes — but now grace has reached the .oor, and the gift is in your open hands.
carry: What are you still trying to pay for?

pulls: God does not justify the godly. He justifies the ungodly — not after they clean up, but while they still cannot.
paras: Where the Dust Lies to You Even after a man hears that salvation is a gift, the dust has one more lie ready: surely the gift is for the godly. Surely God justifies people who are at least heading in the right direction — the ones cleaning up, trying hard, showing promise. And so a man sets to work making himself into the kind of person he assumes grace is for, hoping to qualify for the unqualifiable. He believes in grace in theory, but he is still trying to earn his way into the group he thinks grace is offered to. He has moved the finish line, but he is still running.

Then Paul writes a phrase so scandalous it should stop a man’s breath. God “justifies the ungodly” (Romans 4:5). Not the godly. Not the improving. Not the promising. The ungodly. The very people the dust says could never qualify are the exact people God declares righteous — not after they clean up, but while they are still ungodly, on the basis of faith alone. This is not God overlooking a little remaining sin in basically decent people. This is God justifying the ungodly as ungodly, crediting righteousness to those who have none, the moment they stop working and simply believe.

If that offends something in you, good — it means you have understood it. Grace for the deserving is not grace at all; it is wages. The gospel is not that God helps those who help themselves, but that God justifies those who cannot help themselves at all. And here is the mercy that should make a tired man weep: you do not have to become godly first. You come ungodly, with nothing, and you are declared righteous on the spot — not because of what you are, but because of Whom you believe.

Wages or Gift — You Cannot Have Both Paul sets two columns side by side and they cannot be mixed. “to him who works, the reward is not counted as grace, but as something owed” — that is the works-road, where God owes you what you earned. “to him who doesn’t work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is accounted for righteousness” — that is the faith-road, where God gives what you could never earn. A wage is a debt the employer must pay; a gift is grace the giver freely bestows. And the two are mutually exclusive. The instant you treat your standing with God as a wage you have earned, you have stepped off the gift entirely, because a thing cannot be both owed and given.

This is why the man still trying to qualify for grace has not yet received it. As long as he is working, he is asking God for wages, and wages leave no room for a gift. But the moment he stops working — not stops obeying, but stops trying to earn his standing — and simply believes, the whole transaction changes from payroll to present. The dust wants you in the wages column, forever calculating whether you have done enough. The gospel moves you to the gift column, where the calculating stops, because the righteousness was never something you were owed. It was always something He gave.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: Abraham Believed, and It Was Counted
paras: Paul reaches back to the father of the faith to prove the gift is older than the Law. “Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness” (Romans 4:3, quoting Genesis 15:6). Note when this happened: before circumcision, before the Law was given at Sinai, before Abraham had done a single work of the covenant. God made a promise, Abraham believed it, and on the basis of that belief alone God credited him with righteousness. The righteousness was not earned by Abraham’s obedience; it was reckoned to his faith. The greatest man in Israel’s history was justified exactly the way you are — by believing God, not by working for Him.

This matters enormously, because it means the gospel is not a later, easier arrangement God invented when the Law failed. It was the original plan all along. Abraham was justified by faith centuries before Sinai, which means the Law was never the way in — faith always was. The man who thinks he must keep the Law to be justified has the whole history backwards. Long before there was a Law to keep, there was a God who justified a man for believing a promise. You are not on a lesser path than the patriarchs. You are on the same path Abraham walked: empty hands, open heart, a promise believed, and righteousness credited.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: The Blessing of the Man Whose Sin Is Not Counted
paras: Paul brings in David next, and David adds a second word to “counted”: not only is righteousness counted to the believer, but sin is no longer counted against him. “Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man whom the Lord will by no means charge with sin” (Romans 4:7–8, quoting Psalm 32). There are two ledgers, and grace settles both. In one, a righteousness you did not earn is credited to your account. In the other, the sins you did commit are not charged against you. Christ’s record goes onto your page; your record comes off.

Sit with the word David uses: blessed. Not relieved, not let off, not tolerated — blessed, happy, the most fortunate of men. The man whose sins God refuses to count is not scraping by on a technicality; he is the happiest man alive, because the one thing that could ever condemn him has been taken off the books for good. This is the double cure for the dust of guilt: not only is there no condemnation hanging over you, there is positive righteousness credited to you. You are not at zero, debt cancelled and account empty. You are in the black, rich with a righteousness you never earned, blessed beyond reckoning by a God who will not count your sin.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: The Ruler’s Mirror Image
paras: Remember the rich young ruler, who came working — “I have observed all these things” — and walked away sorrowful, still in the wages column, unable to receive a gift while clutching his earnings. Now set him beside the man of Romans 4:5, “to him who doesn’t work, but believes,” who goes home justified. They are mirror images. The ruler had everything and gained nothing, because he came to God as a worker demanding his due. The believing sinner has nothing and gains everything, because he comes to God with empty hands and simply trusts. The difference between them is not the size of the résumé. It is the direction of the open hand.

And here is the merciful turn for every man who has played the ruler: his story is not the only ending available to you. Where he walked away clutching his works, you can drop yours and stay. Where he came demanding wages, you can come receiving a gift. The very goodness the ruler trusted in was the thing that tripped him; the very emptiness you fear is the thing that qualifies you for grace, because God justifies the ungodly, not the deserving. You do not need a better résumé than the ruler’s. You need to do the one thing he would not: open your hand, let the works fall, and believe.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: From Dust to the Unearned Wage
paras: Psalm 119:25 cries from the floor: “My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word.” (NKJV) And the reviving word this week is the most unlikely good news of all: that God justifies the ungodly. You do not have to climb out of the dust to qualify. The dust is the qualification — not the dust itself, but the empty-handed faith of a man who has stopped pretending he can climb. Revival comes to the man who quits the wages column, stops calculating whether he has earned enough, and simply believes the God who credits righteousness to those who have none. The ungodly man, believing, goes home justified. That is you, this morning, if you will have it.

So this week, when the dust insists the gift must be for better men than you, answer it with Romans 4:5: He justifies the ungodly. When you catch yourself trying to qualify, to clean up first, to earn your way into the group you think grace is for, stop — and remember that grace was never offered to the qualified. It was offered to the bankrupt, the empty-handed, the ungodly who believe. Lift your eyes off your own résumé, drop the works the ruler could not release, and open your hand to the God who counts faith as righteousness and refuses to count your sin. You are not too far gone for this gift. Being far gone is exactly who it is for.

stations.verse: Now to him who works, the reward is not counted as grace, but as something owed. But to him who doesn’t work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is accounted for righteousness.
stations.question: Am I coming to God this week as a worker demanding wages, or as a believer receiving a gift?
stations.gloss: wages, pay, reward
stations.live: Notice one place this week where you expect God to pay you for good behavior. Trade the wage for the gift.
body: Misthos is a wage — what is owed to a man who has worked. Paul uses it on purpose: “to him who works, the reward is not counted as grace, but as something owed.” A wage is earned, and the employer owes it. Grace cannot be owed. Then comes the turn: “to him who doesn’t work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly.” You cannot be paid for your salvation and be given it at the same time.

stations.verse: Blessed is he whose disobedience is forgiven, whose sin is covered. Blessed is the man to whom Yahweh doesn’t impute iniquity, in whose spirit there is no deceit.
stations.question: What sin am I still covering myself, instead of confessing it and letting God cover it?
stations.gloss: to cover, to conceal
stations.live: Stop covering one sin this week. Confess it plainly, and let God be the One who covers it.
body: Kāsāh means to cover. David says, “Blessed is he whose disobedience is forgiven, whose sin is covered.” A few verses later he uses the same verb for the opposite: “I didn’t hide my iniquity” (Psalm 32:5). This is the exchange. The man who stops covering his own sin finds God covering it. As long as you hide it, you carry it. When you confess it, God covers it for good.

stations.verse: ‘Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man whom the Lord will by no means charge with sin.’
stations.question: Do I live as a “blessed” man whose sin God refuses to count?
stations.gloss: blessed, happy, fortunate
stations.live: Stop reading your old ledger to yourself. God will not charge you with those sins. Close the book He closed.
body: Makarios is the word of the Beatitudes: blessed, deeply and enviably happy. Paul quotes David: “Blessed is the man whom the Lord will by no means charge with sin.” The forgiven man is not meant to creep around relieved that he escaped. He is meant to walk in the settled joy of a man whose sins are off the books. Grace does not leave you grateful but anxious. It makes you blessed.

stations.verse: For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not toward God. For what does the Scripture say? ‘Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness.’
stations.question: What in my own record am I tempted to point to before God?
stations.gloss: a ground for boasting, something to boast about
stations.live: Catch yourself this week when you start listing your record before God. Stop, and name Christ instead.
body: Kauchēma is a reason to boast — something a man can point to. Paul says, “if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not toward God.” Abraham had a record among men, and it counted for nothing before God. What counted was that he “believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness.” Nobody stands before God pointing at his own record. Every man there points to Christ.

stations.verse: For this cause it is of faith, that it may be according to grace, to the end that the promise may be sure to all the offspring, not to that only which is of the law, but to that also which is of the faith of Abraham, who is the father of us all.
stations.question: Why does my security depend on faith and not works?

stations.verse: Even as Abraham ‘believed God, and it was counted to him for righteousness.’
stations.question: Where am I treating my faith-walk as a lesser path than the disciplined keepers of the Law, when Abraham himself walked by faith?

stations.verse: And if by grace, then it is no longer of works; otherwise grace is no longer grace. But if it is of works, it is no longer grace; otherwise work is no longer work.
stations.question: Where am I quietly mixing grace and works?

stations.verse: But God, being rich in mercy, for his great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead through our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ—by grace you have been saved—
stations.question: “Even when we were dead” — do I grasp that grace met me at my deadest, not my best, and rest in that?
stations.gloss: to make alive together with
stations.live: Tell God tonight where you were dead when He found you. Thank Him that He made you alive with Christ.
body: Syzōopoieō means to make alive together. Paul says God, “even when we were dead through our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ.” He says it again to the Colossians: “He made you alive together with him” (Colossians 2:13). Grace did not wait for you to improve. It met you dead, and it did not raise you alone. It raised you together with Christ, so that His life is now yours.
pulls: The ruler had everything and gained nothing, clutching his wages. The empty-handed believer has nothing and gains everything. The di)erence is the direction of the open hand.

practices.title: FIND OUT WHICH COLUMN YOU LIVE IN
practices.body: Wages or gift — you cannot have both. This week, examine your prayers: are you presenting work and expecting God to pay (“I read, I served, I resisted — so surely now…”), or receiving freely (“I bring nothing; I believe”)? Each time you catch yourself in the wages column, move over: “My standing is a gift, not a wage. I stop calculating and start receiving.”

practices.title: COME UNGODLY, DON’T CLEAN UP FIRST
practices.body: The dust says: get yourself presentable, then approach God. Reverse it. This week, when you are at your worst and least “godly,” come immediately, exactly then: “Lord, you justify the ungodly — so you justify me right now, as I am, not after I fix myself.” The instinct to clean up before coming is the works-road in disguise. Come as you are, because that is the only way anyone comes.

practices.title: LEAN YOUR WEIGHT ON THE SON
practices.body: Faith is not a work; it is leaning. This week, picture Abraham leaning his whole future on a promise, and do the same with Christ: “Lord, I am not performing for you. I am leaning my whole weight on you. Hold me up — that is all faith is.” When you feel the urge to prove yourself, replace it with the lean. God counts the lean as righteousness.

practices.title: LET THE SPIRIT CLOSE THE OLD LEDGER
practices.body: A forgiven man often keeps reading his own old ledger of sins. This week, when the accusing list reopens, ask the Spirit to shut it: “Holy Spirit, God said He will not count these against me. Help me stop counting what He has stopped counting. Make me a blessed man, not an anxious one.” Let Him train you to walk in the settled joy of the man whose sin is uncounted.

practices.title: TELL A BROTHER YOU CAME UNGODLY
practices.body: Shame makes a man hide until he feels worthy, which is never. Before the week ends, tell a trusted brother that you came to God this week ungodly and empty-handed and were received — and remind each other that grace was never for the deserving. Saying it out loud breaks the private lie that you must qualify first, and anchors you both in the God who justifies the ungodly.

title: The God Who Justifies the Ungodly
subtitle: from dust to the unearned wage
keyVerse: But to him who doesn’t work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is accounted for righteousness.

passage.text: What then will we say that Abraham, our forefather, has found according to the flesh?
For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not toward God.
For what does the Scripture say? “Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness.”
Now to him who works, the reward is not counted as grace, but as something owed.
But to him who doesn’t work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is accounted for righteousness.
Even as David also pronounces blessing on the man to whom God counts righteousness apart from works,
“Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, whose sins are covered.
Blessed is the man whom the Lord will by no means charge with sin.”

stationsLabel: THE WORD ON JUSTIFYING THE UNGODLY
stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Let the verse land first, then answer honestly — and where a Greek word is opened up, let it sharpen the verse you just prayed over.
lifeIntro: This week is not about becoming godly enough by Friday. It is about coming ungodly, with empty hands, to the God who justifies exactly that kind of man.
prayer: Father, You justify the ungodly. I come as one, with nothing in my hands. I stop covering my sin, and I confess it to You. Cover it, as You have promised. Thank You that You will not charge it to me. Make me a blessed man, not an anxious one. You made me alive with Christ when I was dead. I believe You. Amen.

I come as one, with nothing in my hands.
I stop covering my sin, and I confess it to You.
Cover it, as You have promised.
Thank You that You will not charge it to me.
