bottomLine: God justifies the ungodly. A wage is owed to the man who works, but righteousness is credited to the man who believes. The blessed man is not the man with the best record. He is the man whose sin is covered and whom the Lord will not charge with sin.
benediction: Brother, the dust has one lie left after grace itself: that the gift must be for better men — the godly, the improving, the ones with promise — and surely not for someone as ungodly as you have been. Lift your eyes off that lie and onto the most scandalous phrase in the letter: God justifies the ungodly. Not after they clean up. Not once they show promise. While they are still ungodly, still weak, still sinners, He credits righteousness to their faith and refuses to count their sin. The very thing you were sure disqualified you is the exact condition the gift was made for.

So this week, when you are at your worst and the dust says wait until you are worthy, lift up your eyes and come anyway. When you catch yourself in the wages column, calculating whether you have earned enough, lift up your eyes and move to the gift. When the old ledger of your sins reopens and you start reading it to yourself, lift up your eyes to the God who said He will not count them, and close the book He closed. The rich young ruler came clutching his works and walked away with nothing; but you can drop the works he could not release, open your empty hand, and lean your whole weight on Christ — and the God who justifies the ungodly will count your faith as righteousness and call you, of all things, blessed.

This is from dust to revival — not a man climbing out of the dust to qualify for grace, but a man discovering that empty-handed faith in the dust is exactly what grace was looking for. Christ died for the ungodly while they were still ungodly; God credits righteousness to those who have none; the man with nothing in his hands but trust goes home justified. Lift up your eyes off your own résumé and onto the God who keeps the pen and writes “righteous” over the account of everyone who simply believes. You are not too far gone. Being far gone, and knowing it, and leaning anyway — that is the whole of saving faith. Welcome to week six, where the ungodly go home justified.
closingVerse: Your soul clings to the dust, sure the gift is for better men. Lift up your eyes — God justifies the ungodly, and the empty hand that simply leans goes home counted righteous.
carry: What sin are you still covering yourself?

pulls: If Peter could drift back toward works, so can you. The gospel is not a decision you made once — it is the road you are pulled back onto, again and again, by grace.
paras: Where the Dust Lies to You There is a quiet drift that happens to even the most grace-soaked man, and it happened to the greatest apostle of them all. Peter had eaten freely with the Gentile believers, living in the open air of the gospel, until the men from the circumcision party showed up — and then, out of fear of what they would think, Peter pulled back. He withdrew from the table. He started performing again. Not because he had abandoned Christ, but because the old gravity of works and approval pulled his feet back onto a road he knew better than to walk.

Paul names it for what it was: their conduct “didn’t walk uprightly according to the truth of the Good News” (Galatians 2:14). And then he says to Peter’s face, in front of everyone, the truth this whole week turns on: “a man is not justified by the works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ” (Galatians 2:16). This is the sobering, merciful point. If Peter — who walked with Jesus, who preached at Pentecost, who knew grace as well as any man alive — could drift back toward works, then so can you, and you should stop imagining you are above it. The pull back to performance is not a beginner’s problem you graduate from. It is a lifelong gravity, and the gospel is the only thing strong enough to keep pulling you back into step.

So this week is not about a one-time decision you made years ago. It is about the daily realignment every believer needs — the constant, gentle correction back onto the road of faith when your feet drift toward works. And the good news buried in Peter’s failure is this: the same gospel that straightened the rock’s path is strong enough to straighten yours, every single time you notice the drift and turn back. You are not disqualified by the drift. You are simply, like Peter, invited to get back in step.

The Verdict Already Rendered The word at the center of this week is one of the great words of the gospel: justified. It is a courtroom word. To be justified is to have the Judge Himself declare you righteous — not to be made gradually better, but to be pronounced, by verdict, in the right. And Paul says it three times in a single verse: a man is not justified by works of the law but through faith; you believed in Christ Jesus to be justified by faith and not by works; because by works of the law no one will be justified. Three times, as if to nail the courtroom door shut against the works- road forever.

This changes the entire posture of a man’s life. The man trusting his works lives forward, always trying to earn a verdict that has not yet been spoken, anxious about a trial still pending. The man trusting Christ lives backward from a verdict already rendered — declared righteous, the gavel already fallen, the case already closed. You are not working toward an acquittal. In Christ, you are working out from one. And nothing you do this week, good or bad, reopens a case the Judge has already settled by faith.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: The Substitute the Law Required
paras: Why can no one be justified by works of the law? Because the Law demands a perfection no fallen man can produce, and it accepts nothing less. The Law was never looking for effort or improvement or a good-faith attempt; it required a flawless record, and there was only ever one way for a guilty man to have one — a Substitute. The law can take a man as far as Calvary and not one step further, because its whole work is to show him he needs Someone to keep it in his place. Paul says it plainly: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). He did not lower the Law’s demand. He met it, and then He bore its curse.

This is the heart of substitution, and it is the only thing that makes the verdict possible. Christ kept the Law you could never keep — the active obedience that earns the righteous verdict — and then took the curse your law-breaking earned — the death that satisfies the sentence. Both halves are credited to you by faith: His perfect record becomes your righteousness, His death becomes your acquittal. You are not justified because you finally did enough. You are justified because Another did everything, in your place, and the verdict rendered over Him is now rendered over you. The Substitute is the whole reason a guilty man can stand acquitted.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: Crucified With Christ, So the Old Striver Is Dead
paras: Then Paul says one of the most freeing sentences a striving man can hear: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). The man who was trying to justify himself — the performer, the calculator, the one forever auditioning before God — that man was crucified with Christ. He died. The life Paul now lives, he lives by faith in the Son of God, not by the frantic effort of the old self. The striver is not being slowly reformed; he was put to death, and a new life has risen in his place — a life lived by faith from start to finish.

This is why the return to works is not just unwise but, in a sense, a resurrection of a corpse. When you slide back onto the works-road, you are dragging the dead man out of the grave and asking him to perform again. But he is dead. You do not owe him your obedience anymore. The life you live now is Christ’s life in you, received and lived by faith, not the old self’s exhausting attempt to earn what Christ already secured. When the old striver tries to climb back into the driver’s seat this week, you can tell him the truth: that man was crucified with Christ, and the life I now live, I live by faith.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: The One Sin That Empties the Cross
paras: Paul ends the passage with a warning so sharp it should make every performer tremble: “I don’t reject the grace of God. For if righteousness is through the law, then Christ died for nothing!” (Galatians 2:21). Think about what he is saying. If a man could be made righteous by keeping the law — by his own performance, even partly — then the cross was unnecessary. Christ would have died for nothing. Every time you drift back to earning your standing, you are quietly implying that the cross was not enough, that Calvary needs your contribution to complete it. To add your works to Christ’s finished work is not humble; it is to empty His death of its meaning.

But hear the mercy underneath the warning. The reason works-righteousness empties the cross is that the cross was already full — complete, sufficient, lacking nothing. You are not insulting Christ by trying to help; you are missing the staggering relief that there is nothing left to add. The whole price was paid. The verdict was secured. When you stop trying to contribute, you are not being lazy — you are honoring the sufficiency of what He did. The cross does not need your works, and that is the best news a tired man ever heard: Christ did not die to get you started. He died to finish it.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: From Dust to the Verdict
paras: Psalm 119:25 cries from the floor: “My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word.” (NKJV) And the reviving word this week is a verdict already spoken: justified, by faith, not by works. Revival, for a man who keeps drifting back to earning, comes not when he finally performs his way to a verdict, but when he rests in the verdict already rendered over him in Christ. The man crucified with Christ does not crawl back to the works-road to prove himself; he lives out, by faith, the acquittal he already has. The dust says the trial is still pending. The Word says the gavel already fell, and the word over you is righteous.

So this week, when you catch your feet drifting back toward performance — as Peter’s did, as every believer’s do — do not panic and do not despair. Simply notice the drift and step back into the gospel. Remind the old striver that he was crucified with Christ. Refuse to nullify grace by adding your works to a finished cross. The Substitute kept the Law you could not keep and bore the curse you earned, and the verdict over Him is now the verdict over you. Lift your eyes off your own performance and onto the One who lived, died, and rose to render you righteous — and then get back in step with the gospel, the only road that was ever going home.

stations.verse: ‘We, being Jews by nature, and not Gentile sinners, yet knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, even we believed in Christ Jesus, that we might be justified by faith in Christ, and not by the works of the law, because no flesh will be justified by the works of the law.
stations.question: Paul says it three times in one verse — not by works. Where am I still quietly trusting my works for a verdict Christ already rendered by faith?
stations.gloss: sinner, sinful
stations.live: Stop sorting men into sinners and the rest. Stand in line with every other man — and look to Christ.
body: Hamartōlos is the plain word for a sinner. Paul quotes the easy line men drew in his day: “We, being Jews by nature, and not Gentile sinners.” Then he takes the line away. Even the man born inside the covenant knows “that a man is not justified by the works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ.” There is no class of men who are not sinners. There is only one way any man is justified.

stations.verse: But if while we sought to be justified in Christ, we ourselves also were found sinners, is Christ a servant of sin? Certainly not!
stations.question: Where have I been treating grace as permission instead of freedom?
stations.gloss: servant, attendant, one who serves
stations.live: When you are tempted to treat grace as permission, remember whose servant Christ is. He served to set you free.
body: Diakonos is a servant. Paul asks a sharp question: if men who seek to be justified in Christ are still found to be sinners, “is Christ a servant of sin? Certainly not!” The worry is that grace makes sin cheap. Paul will not have it. Christ is not a servant who waits on your sin. He is the Lord who taught that “whoever wants to become great among you shall be your servant” (Mark 10:43), and who served to free you from sin.

stations.verse: For if I build up again those things which I destroyed, I prove myself a law-breaker.
stations.question: What part of the old works-road have I started building again since I came to Christ?
stations.gloss: to tear down, to destroy
stations.live: Name one brick of the old road you have been putting back in place. Leave it on the ground.
body: Katalyō means to tear down — the word Jesus uses when He says no stone of the temple will be left on another (Matthew 24:2). Paul uses it of the law as a way of standing before God: “if I build up again those things which I destroyed, I prove myself a law-breaker.” You tore down the works-road when you came to Christ. To go back and rebuild it is not humility. It is building again what God told you to leave in rubble.

stations.verse: For before some people came from James, he ate with the Gentiles. But when they came, he drew back and separated himself, fearing those who were of the circumcision. And the rest of the Jews joined him in his hypocrisy, so that even Barnabas was carried away with their hypocrisy.
stations.question: Where am I going along with the room instead of walking in step with the gospel?
stations.gloss: to join in playing a part, to join in hypocrisy
stations.live: Ask yourself where you are playing a part this week to fit the room. Take your seat where the gospel puts you.
body: Synypokrinomai means to play a part alongside someone — to join in the pretense. Paul says that when Peter drew back from the Gentile believers, “the rest of the Jews joined him in his hypocrisy, so that even Barnabas was carried away with their hypocrisy.” The word appears nowhere else in the New Testament. One good man’s drift became a whole table’s act. Nobody had changed his doctrine. Everybody had changed his seat.

stations.verse: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us. For it is written, ‘Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree,’
stations.question: Christ became the curse I earned — do I live as a man whose curse has been carried, or as one still trying to lift it myself?

stations.verse: We maintain therefore that a man is justified by faith apart from the works of the law.
stations.question: “Apart from works” — where am I still secretly adding my works to faith as the basis of my standing with God?
stations.gloss: apart from, without
stations.live: Say both sentences this week: “I am justified apart from my works,” and “Apart from Christ I can do nothing.”
body: Chōris means apart from — without. Paul uses it in his plainest sentence: “a man is justified by faith apart from the works of the law.” He used it seven verses earlier too: “But now apart from the law, a righteousness of God has been revealed” (Romans 3:21). Jesus uses it of the branch: “apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). Justification is apart from your works. Fruit is never apart from Christ.

stations.verse: Being therefore justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ;
stations.question: Justification brings peace?

stations.verse: and be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own, that which is of the law, but that which is through faith in Christ, the righteousness which is from God by faith,
stations.question: Which righteousness am I leaning on this week — my own performance, or the righteousness from God that comes through faith?
pulls: If righteousness were through the law, Christ died for no purpose. The cross does not need your works — and that is the best news a tired man ever heard.

practices.title: WATCH FOR THE FLINCH
practices.body: Peter’s drift began with a flinch — fear of what others would think. This week, watch for your own: the moment you pull back toward performing because of someone’s opinion, or perform harder to win approval. Name it: “That is the flinch that pulled Peter off the gospel.” Then step back: “I am justified by faith, not by their approval or my performance.” The drift starts small; catch it small.

practices.title: LIVE FROM THE VERDICT, NOT TOWARD IT
practices.body: This week, notice whether you are living forward (anxiously trying to earn a verdict) or backward (resting in one already rendered). Each time you catch the forward-anxious posture, turn around: “The gavel already fell. I am declared righteous in Christ. I am not on trial today.” Work, serve, and obey out of the acquittal, not for it. The verdict is behind you, not ahead.

practices.title: TELL THE OLD STRIVER HE IS DEAD
practices.body: When the old self-justi.er climbs back into the driver’s seat this week — calculating, performing, auditioning before God — do not negotiate with him. Tell him the truth: “You were crucified with Christ. I owe you nothing. The life I live now, I live by faith in the Son of God.” Then take your hands off the performance and let Christ live His life through you.

practices.title: REFUSE TO NULLIFY THE CROSS
practices.body: When you fail this week, your instinct will be to add a penance, a harder effort, a contribution to make things right. Reverse it. Ask the Spirit to keep you from nullifying grace: “Holy Spirit, the cross was already full. Keep me from trying to add my works to a finished work. Let me rest in what Christ completed, not insult it by trying to help.” Resting fully is how you honor the cross.

practices.title: BE THE BROTHER WHO SPEAKS THE GOSPEL
practices.body: Peter needed Paul to say it to his face. Some brother near you is drifting back toward works right now and cannot see it. Before the week ends, be willing to do for him what Paul did for Peter — gently, in love, point out the drift and remind him of the verdict. And invite him to do the same for you. You and a brother keep each other in step with the gospel by speaking it out loud.

title: Not Justified by Works of the Law
subtitle: from dust to the verdict
keyVerse: yet knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, even we believed in Christ Jesus, that we might be justified by faith in Christ, and not by the works of the law, because no flesh will be justified by the works of the law.

passage.text: But when Peter came to Antioch, I resisted him to his face, because he stood condemned.
For before some people came from James, he ate with the Gentiles. But when they came, he drew back and separated himself, fearing those who were of the circumcision.
And the rest of the Jews joined him in his hypocrisy, so that even Barnabas was carried away with their hypocrisy.

But when I saw that they didn’t walk uprightly according to the truth of the Good News, I said to Peter before them all, “If you, being a Jew, live as the Gentiles do, and not as the Jews do, why do you compel the Gentiles to live as the Jews do?
“We, being Jews by nature, and not Gentile sinners,

yet knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, even we believed in Christ Jesus, that we might be justified by faith in Christ, and not by the works of the law, because no flesh will be justified by the works of the law.
But if while we sought to be justified in Christ, we ourselves also were found sinners, is Christ a servant of sin? Certainly not!
For if I build up again those things which I destroyed, I prove myself a law-breaker.
For I, through the law, died to the law, that I might live to God.

I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.
I don’t reject the grace of God. For if righteousness is through the law, then Christ died for nothing!”

stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Let the verse land first, then answer honestly — and where a Greek word is opened up, let it sharpen the verse you just prayed over.
lifeIntro: This week is not about never drifting again by Friday. It is about catching the drift, like Peter, and stepping back into the verdict already rendered.
prayer: Lord, I am a sinner like every other man. I am justified by faith in Christ, apart from my works. Forgive me for the times I have gone back to the old road. Forgive me for playing a part to fit the room. Keep my feet walking uprightly in the truth of the gospel. Christ loved me and gave Himself up for me. I live by faith in Him. Amen.
prayerLines: Lord, I am a sinner like every other man.
I am justified by faith in Christ, apart from my works.
Forgive me for the times I have gone back to the old road.
Forgive me for playing a part to fit the room.
Keep my feet walking uprightly in the truth of the gospel.
Christ loved me and gave Himself up for me.
I live by faith in Him. Amen.
bottomLine: A man is not justified by the works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ. Peter drifted, and a whole table followed him, but the gospel called him back. You were crucified with Christ; to rebuild the works-road is to treat His death as if it were for nothing.
benediction: Brother, the dust does not only trip the new believer; it pulls at the feet of the strongest saint alive. It happened to Peter — the rock, the preacher of Pentecost, the man who knew grace as well as anyone — who drew back from the gospel table out of fear of what others would think, and slipped, just like that, back toward performance. Lift your eyes off your own drifting feet. If the rock could drift, you are in humble company, and there is no shame in needing the gospel preached to you again. The same word that straightened Peter’s path is strong enough to straighten yours, today and every day you notice the pull and turn back.

So when your feet drift toward earning this week, lift up your eyes. When fear of someone’s opinion makes you flinch back into performing, lift up your eyes. When you fail and reach for a penance to make it right, lift up your eyes to the cross that was already full, and refuse to nullify by your works what Christ completed by His blood. The Law required a flawless record and a Substitute to provide it, and Christ gave both — He kept the Law you could not keep and bore the curse you earned, and the verdict rendered over Him is now rendered over you. You are not awaiting trial. The gavel has fallen. The word is righteous.

This is from dust to revival — not a man performing his way to a verdict, but a man resting in the verdict already spoken over him in Christ. The old striver who lived to justify himself was crucified with Christ; the life you live now, you live by faith in the Son of God who loved you and gave Himself for you. Lift up your eyes off your own performance and onto the Substitute who lived, died, and rose to declare you righteous — and then step back into the gospel, the only road that was ever going home. The cross does not need your works. It needs only your trust. Welcome to week seven of living from the verdict, not toward it.
closingVerse: Your soul clings to the dust, dragging the old striver back to work. Lift up your eyes — he was crucified with Christ, and the verdict over you is already righteous.
carry: Where have your feet drifted from the gospel?

pulls: You did not begin the Christian life by works. So why try to finish it by works? The grace that saved you is the grace that sustains you.
paras: Where the Dust Lies to You One of the strangest things about the Christian life is something nearly every man does. He comes to Christ by grace — empty-handed, believing, receiving a gift he could never earn — and then, somewhere along the way, he quietly switches roads. Having started the Christian life by faith, he sets about finishing it by works. He received salvation as a gift but now tries to maintain it as a wage. He began leaning entirely on Christ and now leans, more and more, on his own effort, his discipline, his performance. He started in the Spirit, and he is trying to be completed in the flesh.

Paul finds this so baffling he can only call it a kind of spell: “Foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you” (Galatians 3:1). And then the question that exposes the whole confusion: “Having begun in the Spirit, are you now completed in the flesh?” (Galatians 3:3). It is as absurd, Paul says, as a man who was born and then tries to keep himself alive by his own manufacturing — as if the life he received as a gift could now be sustained by his own production. You did not begin the Christian life by works, and you cannot continue it by works. The same grace that saved you is the grace that sustains you. The same faith that started you is the faith that finishes you.

So this week confronts a drift so common most men never notice it: the slow slide from faith back to flesh, from receiving to producing, from the Spirit’s work to your own. And the cure is not condemnation — Paul calls them foolish, but he is pleading for them, not against them. The cure is to remember how it all began. You came with nothing and received everything. Nothing has changed. The Christian life is not earned after it is given; it is lived, from first breath to last, the same way it started — by the Spirit, through faith, leaning wholly on Christ.

Begun by the Spirit Paul anchors his argument in their own experience: “Did you receive the Spirit by the works of the law, or by hearing of faith?” (Galatians 3:2). They knew the answer. The Spirit came to them not when they achieved enough but when they believed the gospel they heard. The whole supernatural reality of their new life — the Spirit indwelling them, transforming them, bearing fruit in them — began by faith, not by performance. And Paul’s point is devastatingly simple: if the Spirit came by faith, He continues by faith. You do not switch engines halfway. The power that started your Christian life is the only power that can carry it on.

This is the death of the exhausting do-it-yourself sanctification that wears so many men down. The dust says: God got you started, now it is up to you to keep it going by sheer effort. But the gospel says the Spirit who began the work is the One who continues it, and your part is not to manufacture growth by willpower but to keep walking in the same faith that received Him in the first place. Growth is not the flesh straining to improve; it is the Spirit bearing fruit in a man who keeps leaning on Christ. You are not the engine. You never were. You are the branch, and the life flows from the Vine.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: The Spell of Self-Effort
paras: Why does Paul reach for the word bewitched? Because the drift back to works is not rational — it is a kind of enchantment that makes a man act against everything he knows to be true. He knows he was saved by grace. He knows he contributed nothing. And yet some spell convinces him that, going forward, his standing rises and falls with his performance. The fog of self-effort settles over him so gradually he does not notice it has happened, until one day he realizes he is exhausted, anxious, and measuring God’s favor by the quality of his week — living, in other words, exactly as he did before he was saved.

The breaking of the spell is not a new technique or a harder push. It is a clear-eyed look back at how the whole thing began. Paul does not tell the Galatians to try harder or to try less; he tells them to remember. Remember that the Spirit came by faith. Remember that you received and did not achieve. Remember that the cross was a gift. The spell of self- effort is broken by the memory of grace — and the moment a man recalls that he began with empty hands, he can open them again, and the fog lifts. You are not bewitched forever. The truth you already know is enough to break the spell.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: The Vow at Sinai, the Same Mistake Again
paras: This is not a new error; it is the oldest one in the book. At Sinai the people heard the Law and vowed, “All the words which Yahweh has spoken will we do” (Exodus 24:3) — and the vow of we will do collapsed at the golden calf before Moses even came down the mountain. The Galatians were making the same mistake centuries later, and you make it still. We will do is the 8esh’s reflex in every age — the confident assumption that you can carry by your own effort what only God can sustain. And it always breaks, because the flesh has no power to perfect what the Spirit began.

The Galatians had received the Spirit and then turned back to the very thing that failed Israel at Sinai: the 8esh’s vow to do. But the answer to the broken vow was never a better vow; it was the blood of a Substitute who did what you could not. Sinai itself preached this, with blood thrown on the people in the same hour as their vow, because God knew the vow would break. So when you catch yourself sliding back into we will do — the grim resolve to perfect yourself by effort — hear the echo of the golden calf and stop. Trade the vow for the truth: He has done. The Spirit who began the work will perfect it, and your part is to lean, not to strain.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: The Bar Only Christ Could Clear
paras: Behind the whole Galatian confusion is the impossible standard of the Law, the bar Jesus set when He said “unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, there is no way you will enter into the Kingdom of Heaven” (Matthew 5:20). The man trying to be completed in the flesh is, whether he knows it or not, trying to clear that bar by his own effort — and it cannot be done. Only one man’s righteousness ever exceeded the Pharisees’: Christ’s. He is the only one who ever kept the Law in full, and His righteousness is received by faith, not produced by flesh. The Galatians were straining to manufacture a righteousness Christ had already given them.

This is the relief hidden in the impossible bar. If perfection were achievable by effort, then the pressure would be on you to achieve it, and you would never know if you had done enough. But because the bar is impossibly high — cleared by Christ alone — the pressure is entirely off your performance and entirely on His finished work. You are not being asked to perfect yourself to a standard the best men alive could not reach. You are asked to rest in the One who reached it for you, and to let His Spirit work His righteousness out in you, degree by degree, the way fruit grows on a living branch. The bar you cannot clear, He cleared — so stop straining, and start abiding.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: From Dust to the Spirit
paras: Psalm 119:25 cries from the floor: “My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word.” (NKJV) And the reviving word this week is a question that breaks the spell: having begun by the Spirit, why are you trying to finish by the flesh? Revival, for a man worn out by do-it- yourself sanctification, comes not when he finally strains hard enough but when he remembers that the Spirit who began the work is the One who carries it on. The dust says: it is up to you now. The Word says: it was never up to you — not at the start, not now, not ever. Lean back into the Spirit, and let the One who started the work finish it.

So this week, when you catch yourself straining to perfect what grace began — measuring God’s favor by your effort, exhausting yourself to maintain a standing you were given for free — stop and remember how it started. You came with empty hands and received the Spirit by faith. Nothing has changed. The same faith that started you is the faith that finishes you, and the same Spirit who came as a gift is the One who bears the fruit. Lift your eyes off your own straining effort and onto the Spirit of the living God, who began a good work in you and will carry it on to completion. Stop being completed in the flesh. Be carried, by the Spirit, all the way home.

stations.verse: Are you so foolish? Having begun in the Spirit, are you now completed in the flesh? Did you suffer so many things in vain, if it is indeed in vain?
stations.question: What has grace already done in me that I am in danger of throwing away by going back to the old road?
stations.gloss: in vain, for nothing, to no purpose
stations.live: Look at what grace has already done in you. Refuse to spend it on a road that leads nowhere.
body: Eikē means in vain — for no purpose. Paul asks the Galatians, “Did you suffer so many things in vain, if it is indeed in vain?” If they go back to the law, everything they suffered for the gospel was for nothing. He uses the word again: “I am afraid for you, that I might have wasted my labor for you” (Galatians 4:11). Going back to the works-road does not add to what grace began. It throws it away.

stations.verse: Foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you not to obey the truth, before whose eyes Jesus Christ was openly portrayed among you as crucified?
stations.question: What “spell” of self-effort has settled over me so gradually I did not notice?
stations.gloss: foolish, without understanding
stations.live: Think it through this week: if you could not start your salvation, why would you try to finish it?
body: Anoētos means without understanding — not thinking it through. Paul calls the Galatians “Foolish Galatians” and then asks, “Are you so foolish?” Jesus uses the same word on the road to Emmaus: “Foolish men, and slow of heart to believe” (Luke 24:25). It is not an insult for sport. It is a wake-up. Men who began with Christ crucified before their eyes were trying to finish by their own effort, and could not see how little sense it made.

stations.verse: He therefore who supplies the Spirit to you and does miracles among you, does he do it by the works of the law, or by hearing of faith?
stations.question: Do I expect God’s ongoing work in me to come by my effort, or by the same hearing-with-faith that started it?
stations.gloss: to supply, to provide generously
stations.live: Start one morning this week by asking God to supply what you need for the day, before you try to supply it yourself.
body: Epichorēgeō means to supply — to provide what is needed, and keep providing it. Paul asks, “He therefore who supplies the Spirit to you and does miracles among you, does he do it by the works of the law, or by hearing of faith?” The verb is ongoing. God did not give the Spirit once and then leave you to run on your own fuel. He keeps supplying, and He supplies by grace received through faith.

stations.verse: Moses came and told the people all Yahweh’s words, and all the ordinances; and all the people answered with one voice, and said, ‘All the words which Yahweh has spoken will we do.’ He took the book of the covenant and read it in the hearing of the people, and they said, ‘We will do all that Yahweh has said, and be obedient.’
stations.question: Where is the old Sinai vow of “we will do” still running my walk with God?

stations.verse: being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ.
stations.question: If God promises to complete what He began, why do I carry the weight of finishing it as though it were mine?

stations.verse: Remain in me, and I in you. As the branch can’t bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you, unless you remain in me. I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.
stations.question: Am I straining like an engine to produce fruit, or abiding like a branch and letting the life flow from the Vine?

stations.verse: The Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the Good News beforehand to Abraham, saying, ‘In you all the nations will be blessed.’
stations.question: How does it change my view of the law to know the gospel was announced to Abraham first?
stations.gloss: to announce good news beforehand
stations.live: Read Genesis 12:3 and Galatians 3:8 together. Thank God that the gospel came before the law.
body: Proeuangelizomai means to preach the good news ahead of time. It appears only here in the New Testament. “The Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the Good News beforehand to Abraham, saying, ‘In you all the nations will be blessed.’” The gospel is not a late fix after the law failed. It was announced to Abraham before the law was ever given. Faith was always the way.

stations.verse: For as many as are of the works of the law are under a curse. For it is written, ‘Cursed is everyone who doesn’t continue in all things that are written in the book of the law, to do them.’
stations.question: Do I live as a man still under the curse, or as a man for whom Christ became a curse?
stations.gloss: cursed, under a curse
stations.live: When the old curse speaks this week, answer it with Galatians 3:13.
body: Epikataratos means cursed — under a curse. Paul quotes the law: “Cursed is everyone who doesn’t continue in all things that are written in the book of the law, to do them.” Three verses later he uses the same word of Christ: “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree” (Galatians 3:13). The curse the law pronounced on you, Christ took on Himself. He was counted cursed so that you could be counted blessed.
pulls: You are not the engine. You are the branch. The life that started in the Spirit is carried on by the Spirit — your part is to abide, not to strain.

practices.title: NAME WHERE YOU SWITCHED ENGINES
practices.body: Most men quietly switch from faith to flesh without noticing. This week, name where it happened for you: “I received this by grace, but now I am trying to maintain it by effort.” Maybe it is your sense of God’s favor, your assurance, your growth. Write it down, then preach Galatians 3:3 over it: “Having begun by the Spirit, I will not try to be completed in the flesh.”

practices.title: BREAK THE SPELL BY REMEMBERING
practices.body: When the fog of “it’s up to me now” settles this week, do not push harder — remember. Look again at how it began: empty hands, a gift received, the Spirit given by faith. Say it: “I contributed nothing at the start, and nothing has changed. The cross was a gift then; it is a gift now.” The spell of self-effort breaks not by trying but by recalling grace.

practices.title: ABIDE IN THE SON INSTEAD OF STRAINING
practices.body: This week, when you feel the urge to manufacture growth by willpower, switch from engine to branch: “Lord, I cannot produce fruit by straining. I abide in you. Let your life flow through me.” Then give real time to abiding — the Word, prayer, beholding Him — and trust that fruit grows on a branch that stays connected, not on one that grits its teeth.

practices.title: LET THE SPIRIT CARRY WHAT YOU CANNOT
practices.body: Ask the Spirit this week to do what the flesh never could: “Holy Spirit, you began this work in me, and you have promised to complete it. I stop trying to be my own engine. Carry me. Bear your fruit in me. Transform me degree by degree as I behold Christ.” Then watch how differently a week goes when you lean instead of strain.

practices.title: TELL A BROTHER WHERE YOU’RE STRIVING
practices.body: The spell of self-effort thrives in isolation, where a man slowly exhausts himself in private. Before the week ends, tell a trusted brother where you have been trying to perfect yourself by the flesh, and ask him to remind you how it all began — by grace, through faith. Sometimes a man cannot see the fog he is in until a brother names it and points him back to the cross.

title: Who Bewitched You?
subtitle: from dust to the Spirit
keyVerse: Are you so foolish? Having begun in the Spirit, are you now completed in the flesh?

passage.text: Foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you not to obey the truth, before whose eyes Jesus Christ was openly portrayed among you as crucified?
I just want to learn this from you: Did you receive the Spirit by the works of the law, or by hearing of faith?
Are you so foolish? Having begun in the Spirit, are you now completed in the flesh?
Did you suffer so many things in vain, if it is indeed in vain?
He therefore who supplies the Spirit to you and does miracles among you, does he do it by the works of the law, or by hearing of faith?
Even as Abraham “believed God, and it was counted to him for righteousness.”
Know therefore that those who are of faith are children of Abraham.
The Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the Good News beforehand to Abraham, saying, “In you all the nations will be blessed.”
So then, those who are of faith are blessed with the faithful Abraham.
For as many as are of the works of the law are under a curse. For it is written, “Cursed is everyone who doesn’t continue in all things that are written in the book of the law, to do them.”
Now that no man is justified by the law before God is evident, for, “The righteous will live by faith.”
The law is not of faith, but, “The man who does them will live by them.”
Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us. For it is written, “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree,”
that the blessing of Abraham might come on the Gentiles through Christ Jesus, that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.

stationsLabel: THE WORD ON THE SPIRIT AND FAITH
stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Let the verse land first, then answer honestly — and where a Greek word is opened up, let it sharpen the verse you just prayed over.
lifeIntro: This week is not about perfecting yourself by Friday. It is about breaking the spell of self- effort and leaning back into the Spirit who began the work.
prayer: Father, I began by Your Spirit. Forgive me for trying to finish by my own strength. You keep supplying Your Spirit to me by grace. Christ became a curse for me, so I am not under one. Keep me from wasting what grace has done. Let me live this week hearing and believing, not straining and proving. Amen.

bottomLine: You began by the Spirit, and you will not be completed by the flesh. God keeps supplying His Spirit by the hearing of faith, not by works. Christ became a curse for you, so the blessing promised to Abraham comes to you through faith.
benediction: Brother, the dust works a quiet spell on a saved man. It lets him begin by grace — empty hands, a gift received, the Spirit given by faith — and then slowly convinces him that the rest is up to him, that he must now maintain by effort what he could never have earned in the first place. Lift your eyes off your own straining. Paul asked the Galatians the question that breaks the spell, and it is for you too: having begun by the Spirit, are you now being completed in the flesh? You did not start this way, and you cannot continue this way. The same grace that saved you is the grace that sustains you, all the way home.

So when the fog of “it’s up to me now” settles over you this week, lift up your eyes. When you find yourself exhausted, measuring God’s favor by the quality of your week, lift up your eyes. When the old Sinai reflex of “we will do” rises and you feel the grim resolve to perfect yourself by willpower, lift up your eyes to the cross that was portrayed plainly before you — Christ crucified, the gift that began it all. The bar of the Law was cleared by Him, not by you; the Spirit came by faith, not by works; and the One who began a good work in you has promised to bring it to completion. You are not the engine. You are the branch, and the life flows from the Vine.

This is from dust to revival — not a man straining to finish by the flesh what grace began by the Spirit, but a man who remembers how it started and leans back into the One who carries it on. Stop trying to be your own engine. Stop dragging the dead weight of self-effort up a hill the Spirit was always going to climb for you. Lift up your eyes off your own performance and onto the Spirit of the living God, abide like a branch on the Vine, and let Him bear His fruit and finish His work. The spell breaks the moment you remember grace. You began by the Spirit; you will be completed by the Spirit too. Welcome to week eight of being carried, not carrying.
closingVerse: Your soul clings to the dust, exhausted from trying to finish by the .esh. Lift up your eyes — the Spirit who began the work will carry it home.
carry: What are you trying to finish that God began?

pulls: Your standing with God is not a contract you must keep up. It is a promise He made and swore to keep Himself — older than the Law, and unbreakable.
paras: Where the Dust Lies to You The dust loves to make a man feel like his standing with God is conditional — a contract he must keep up his end of, a deal that stays in force only as long as he performs. He reads his relationship with God as an agreement with fine print: God will bless me if I obey, accept me while I behave, keep me as long as I hold up my side. And so he lives anxiously, always aware that a contract can be broken, always feeling that one bad enough failure could void the whole arrangement and leave him with nothing.

Into that anxiety Paul drops a fact of biblical history that changes everything: the promise came first. “A covenant confirmed beforehand by God in Christ, the law, which came four hundred thirty years after, does not annul” (Galatians 3:17). God made His promise to Abraham four hundred and thirty years before the Law was ever given at Sinai. The inheritance was secured by promise long before there was a Law to keep. And a promise is not a contract. A contract says, I will do my part if you do yours. A promise says, I will do this, because I have said so. Your standing with God was never a deal you had to keep up. It was a promise He made and swore to keep Himself.

This is the deep security a man in the dust has been missing. If your relationship with God rested on a contract, then every failure would threaten it, and you would be right to be anxious. But it rests on a promise — older than the Law, unconditional, guaranteed by the character of God who cannot lie. The Law that came later cannot annul the promise that came first. Your inheritance does not hang on your performance. It hangs on God’s word, and God’s word does not break. Lift your eyes: you are not a contractor nervously fulfilling terms. You are an heir, named in a promise that was settled before you were born.

Promise and Law Do Different Jobs Paul will not let promise and Law be confused, because they do completely different jobs. “For if the inheritance is of the law, it is no more of promise; but God has granted it to Abraham by promise” (Galatians 3:18). The two are mutually exclusive as the basis of your inheritance. If you receive it by keeping the Law, then it is wages you earned, and the promise is irrelevant. If you receive it by promise, then it is a gift God gave, and your law- keeping was never the point. You cannot have it both ways. Either your inheritance is a wage you are still earning, or a gift you have already been given — and Paul says, unmistakably, it is a gift, secured by promise.

Then why the Law at all, if the promise came first and does the saving? Paul answers it directly, and you have heard it before: the Law was added because of transgressions, and the law became a tutor to bring men to Christ (Galatians 3:19, 24). The Law was never a rival to the promise or a replacement for it; it was a temporary escort, added to show you your sin and walk you to the One the promise was always about. The Law served the promise. It never replaced it. And now that Christ has come, the tutor has done its job, and the inheritance stands exactly where it always stood — on the promise of God.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: The Promise Came First
paras: Let the timeline sink in, because it dismantles the works-road at the root. God promised Abraham an inheritance, and “Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness” — four hundred and thirty years before Sinai. The foundation of the whole relationship was laid by grace, received by faith, with no Law in sight. When the Law finally came, it arrived as a latecomer onto a foundation already poured. It could not be the basis of the inheritance, because the inheritance was already granted, by promise, centuries earlier.

This is enormously freeing for a man who feels his standing is always provisional. The order of events settles it: grace was first, Law was second, and the second cannot undo the first. Your relationship with God did not begin with a demand that you perform; it began with a promise He made to bless. The Law that came later, with all its requirements, never changed the foundation — it only made the need for the promised Savior unmistakable. You are not standing on a contract that your failures could void. You are standing on a promise that predates every requirement, and the foundation was poured long before you ever stepped onto it.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: An Inheritance, Not a Wage
paras: The word Paul keeps using is inheritance, and the word itself preaches the gospel. An inheritance is not a wage. A son does not earn his inheritance by working for his father; he receives it because of who he is in the family. It comes by relationship, not by labor; by the father’s will, not by the son’s performance. Paul says the inheritance came to Abraham “by promise” (Galatians 3:18), and to you the same way — not as a paycheck you clock in to earn, but as an estate you receive as sons. The whole framework of wages and earning belongs to the works-road. The framework of inheritance belongs to the family.

This is why the anxious, performing posture is so out of place for a child of God. A hired hand frets about his performance because his pay depends on it; if he slacks, he is docked, and if he fails badly enough, he is fired. But a son does not lose his inheritance by having a bad week, because the inheritance was never tied to his productivity — it was tied to his sonship, secured by his father’s promise. When you catch yourself living like a hired hand, anxious that poor performance might cost you everything, remember: you are not an employee on probation. You are a son, named in a promise, and the inheritance is already guaranteed.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: Heirs in Christ, the True Offspring
paras: Paul makes one more move that secures the whole thing: the promise was made to Abraham and to his offspring — and the offspring, Paul says, is ultimately one person: Christ (Galatians 3:16). The promise finds its yes in Him. And then the staggering inclusion: “If you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring and heirs according to promise” (Galatians 3:29). You do not inherit on the strength of your own bloodline or your own performance. You inherit because you are in Christ, the true Offspring, and in Him the promise made to Abraham becomes yours. The inheritance is secured not by your grip on it but by your union with the One in whom every promise is yes.

This is the unshakable ground beneath the promise. If the inheritance depended on you — your faithfulness, your performance, your grip — it would be only as secure as you are, which is to say, not very. But it depends on Christ, and your share of it is held by your union with Him. The promise was guaranteed in the Offspring before you ever believed, and you came into it the moment you were placed in Him by faith. So when the dust whispers that you could lose the inheritance by failing, answer it with your union: I am in Christ, the true Offspring, and the promise is yes in Him. What is held by Christ cannot be lost by me.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: From Dust to the Promise
paras: Psalm 119:25 cries from the floor: “My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word.” (NKJV) And the reviving word this week is promise — not contract, not deal, not terms you must keep. Revival, for a man who feels his standing is always provisional, comes when he discovers that his inheritance was secured by promise God made and swore to keep Himself, centuries before any Law, guaranteed in Christ the true Offspring. The dust says your relationship with God is a contract you might break. The Word says it is a promise God cannot break. And the difference between those two is the difference between a life of anxiety and a life of rest.

So this week, when the dust tells you your standing is conditional — that one failure could void the deal and leave you with nothing — answer it with the timeline of grace. The promise came 430 years before the Law, and the latecomer cannot annul the foundation. You are not a contractor nervously fulfilling terms, one mistake from losing it all. You are an heir, named in a promise, secured in Christ, with an inheritance that was guaranteed before you were born and cannot be undone by your worst week. Lift your eyes off your own performance and onto the promise of the God who cannot lie — and live, at last, like the son and heir you already are.

stations.verse: Now I say this: A covenant confirmed beforehand by God in Christ, the law, which came four hundred thirty years after, does not annul, so as to make the promise of no effect.
stations.question: Do I relate to God as if my relationship with Him were a contract I must keep up, or as a promise He made and keeps Himself?
stations.gloss: to annul, to make void, to cancel
stations.live: Write down one promise of God you are afraid your failures have cancelled. Then read Galatians 3:17 over it.
body: Akyroō means to cancel — to take away something’s force. Paul says the law, which came four hundred thirty years after the promise, “does not annul” it. Jesus uses the same word of men “making void the word of God by your tradition” (Mark 7:13). Nothing that came later can cancel what God promised first. The law did not overwrite the promise to Abraham. The promise still stands.

stations.verse: Brothers, speaking of human terms, though it is only a man’s covenant, yet when it has been confirmed, no one makes it void or adds to it.
stations.question: What conditions have I quietly added to God’s promise?
stations.gloss: to add to, to add provisions to a document
stations.live: Notice the conditions you keep adding to God’s promise — “if I behave,” “if I keep it up.” Cross them out.
body: Epidiatassomai means to add terms to an agreement already made. It appears only here in the New Testament. Paul says even a man’s covenant, once confirmed, is one that “no one makes it void or adds to it.” If that is true of a man’s word, how much more of God’s? The law did not add conditions to the promise. Nobody gets to write fine print into God’s promise after He has signed it.

stations.verse: For if the inheritance is of the law, it is no more of promise; but God has granted it to Abraham by promise.
stations.question: Do I live as a man granted an inheritance, or as a man still trying to earn one?
stations.gloss: to give freely, to grant as a favor
stations.live: Stop treating your place in God’s family as something you have to keep earning. It was granted.
body: Charizomai comes from charis, grace. It means to give freely, as a favor. “God has granted it to Abraham by promise.” Paul uses it again: “how would he not also with him freely give us all things?” (Romans 8:32). An inheritance by law would be earned. An inheritance by promise is granted. Abraham did not earn it, and neither do you. God gives it the way grace always gives.

stations.verse: If you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring and heirs according to promise.
stations.question: If I am Christ’s, I am an heir according to promise — am I living like a guaranteed heir, or like a hired hand on probation?

stations.verse: For the promise to Abraham and to his offspring that he should be heir of the world wasn’t through the law, but through the righteousness of faith. For if those who are of the law are heirs, faith is made void, and the promise is made of no effect.
stations.question: Where am I still trying to secure through law what God promised to give through the righteousness of faith?

stations.verse: In this way God, being determined to show more abundantly to the heirs of the promise the immutability of his counsel, interposed with an oath, that by two immutable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we may have a strong encouragement, who have fled for refuge to take hold of the hope set before us.
stations.question: God bound Himself with an oath so I could be sure — does my heart rest in the impossibility of God lying, or still fear the promise might fail?
stations.gloss: unchangeable, immutable
stations.live: On the day your faith feels weak this week, read Hebrews 6:18. Lean on what does not move.
body: Ametathetos means unchangeable — what cannot be moved or altered. Hebrews uses it twice: God showed “the immutability of his counsel” with an oath, so that “by two immutable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie,” you might have strong encouragement. God’s promise and God’s oath: two things that will not move. Your feelings move. Your record moves. His word does not.

stations.verse: For however many are the promises of God, in him is the ‘Yes.’ Therefore also through him is the ‘Amen’, to the glory of God through us.
stations.question: Every promise is “Yes” in Christ — am I anchoring my security in His finished work, or in my fragile follow-through?
stations.gloss: yes, truly, certainly
stations.live: Name one promise of God you have been treating as a maybe. Say out loud: “In Christ, the answer is yes.”
body: Nai is the plain word for yes. Paul says, “however many are the promises of God, in him is the ‘Yes.’” Every promise God ever made finds its yes in Christ. Jesus told His disciples to let their yes be yes (Matthew 5:37). God’s yes to you is not a maybe that depends on your week. It is spoken in His Son, and it stands.

stations.verse: So you are no longer a bondservant, but a son; and if a son, then an heir of God through Christ.
stations.question: No longer a slave but a son and heir — which identity actually ran my week, the slave’s anxiety or the heir’s security?
pulls: The promise came 430 years before the Law. The latecomer cannot annul the foundation — your inheritance was secured by grace before any requirement existed.

practices.title: NAME THE CONTRACT YOU THINK YOU’RE UNDER
practices.body: Most men carry a quiet contract with God: “He’ll accept me if I perform, keep me as long as I behave.” This week, name the terms you imagine you’re under. Write them down. Then cross them out and write the truth over them: “This was never a contract. It is a promise God made and swore to keep — 430 years before the Law, and it still stands.” Naming the false contract is the first step to resting in the real promise.

practices.title: TRADE HIRED-HAND ANXIETY FOR HEIR’S SECURITY
practices.body: This week, catch yourself living like a hired hand — anxious about output, afraid one bad week could cost you everything. Each time, preach your status: “I am not an employee on probation. I am a son and an heir, and the inheritance comes by promise, not by my productivity.” Then work and serve from belonging, not for it. An heir labors freely; a hireling labors afraid.

practices.title: ANCHOR THE INHERITANCE IN THE SON
practices.body: You will be tempted to secure your standing by your own grip and panic when your grip slips. Reverse it. Anchor it in Christ: “Lord, the inheritance is held by my union with you, the true Offspring, not by my hold on it. Every promise is yes in you. What you hold, I cannot lose.” When the fear of forfeiting rises this week, answer it: I am in Christ, and the promise is yes in Him.

practices.title: LET THE SPIRIT SEAL THE PROMISE TO YOUR HEART
practices.body: A promise believed is steadier than a promise merely known. This week, ask the Spirit to press the promise into you: “Holy Spirit, you are the guarantee of my inheritance. Make this promise real to me — not a doctrine I affirm but a security I rest in. Quiet the contract- anxiety and seal the promise to my heart.” Let Him turn the fact into felt assurance.

practices.title: TELL A BROTHER THE PROMISE CAME FIRST
practices.body: Contract-thinking grows in isolation, where a man privately renegotiates his terms with God every time he fails. Before the week ends, tell a trusted brother where you’ve been treating grace like a contract, and remind each other of the timeline: the promise came first, the Law came later, and the latecomer cannot annul the foundation. Anchor each other in the promise that was settled before either of you was born.

title: The Inheritance by Promise
subtitle: from dust to the promise
keyVerse: For if the inheritance is of the law, it is no more of promise; but God has granted it to Abraham by promise.

passage.text: Brothers, speaking of human terms, though it is only a man’s covenant, yet when it has been confirmed, no one makes it void or adds to it.
Now the promises were spoken to Abraham and to his offspring. He doesn’t say, “To descendants”, as of many, but as of one, “To your offspring”, which is Christ.
Now I say this: A covenant confirmed beforehand by God in Christ, the law, which came four hundred thirty years after, does not annul, so as to make the promise of no effect.
For if the inheritance is of the law, it is no more of promise; but God has granted it to Abraham by promise.
Then why is there the law? It was added because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom the promise has been made. It was ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator.
Now a mediator is not between one, but God is one.
Is the law then against the promises of God? Certainly not! For if there had been a law given which could make alive, most certainly righteousness would have been of the law.
But the Scripture imprisoned all things under sin, that the promise by faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe.
But before faith came, we were kept in custody under the law, confined for the faith which should afterwards be revealed.
So that the law has become our tutor to bring us to Christ, that we might be justified by faith.
But now that faith has come, we are no longer under a tutor.
For you are all children of God, through faith in Christ Jesus.
For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ.
There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free man, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus.
If you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring and heirs according to promise.
